Get our Newsletter! Like many birds, domestic turkeys, including this group at the Smithsonian's National Zoo in Washington, D.C., are social animals. Smithsonian/Brett Kuxhausen 1. Humans have been raising turkeys for thousands of years. Although indigenous peoples in North America have hunted wild turkeys since the end of the last Ice Age, the animals were first domesticated in Mexico around 2,000 years ago. Dinner wasn’t the original goal: archaeological evidence suggests turkeys were initially kept so their feathers could be used in clothing and ceremonial regalia. By A.D. 500, people were raising turkeys in what is now the United States too, judging by archaeological remains from caves in Arizona and New Mexico. Even so, those weren’t the birds that English settlers ate in the Thirteen Colonies. The domestic turkey descends from a southern Mexican bird that the Spanish took home in the 1500s. The birds then spread through Europe, and colonists brought them back across the Atlantic. The bird’s English name may reflect this long-distance trade: turkeys are thought to have reached England along winding trading routes that first passed through the country of Turkey. 2. pages.text: Ten Wildlife Photographers Zoom In on Their Favorite Birds Skip to main content Science | September/October 2023 Ten Wildlife Photographers Zoom In on Their Favorite Birds Get up close and personal with a birder’s-eye view of the United States, as reflected by our beloved feathered neighbors It’s a radiant morning, and the zoo is filled with birds. Robins bathe in a waterfall. Pigeons peck at a discarded slice of pizza. Mallards circle around an artificial pond. Near a fence, strollers pause as chubby fingers point at the flamingos. These creatures from the Caribbean are sleeping—balanced on one leg, long necks twisted backward, bills nestled into cotton-candy feathers. “Everybody loves the colorful ones,” says Sara Hallager , bird curator at the Smithsonian’s National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute . “I happen to like brown ones.” Along the path hops a tiny wood thrush, the official bird of Washington, D.C. “See? Wimbledon champions Patten and Finnish team-mate Harri Heliovaara received their trophy ​from the ATP's chief tour officer Andre Silva in Turin, after ending the season as the top-ranked men's doubles pairing for the first time. In his acceptance speech, Patten, 30, called out ATP chairman Andrea Gaudenzi and CEO ​Eno Polo for their decision not to attend. "What a journey it has been. Turin is such a special place for us, we played a challenger just across the road when we ranked 60 and 40 in the world a couple of years ago. I never would ​have dreamt that we would be in the position that we're in now," said Patten. "For ​us it's a really big deal. ​It's a real shame that the ATP ‌chairman ⁠and the ATP CEO don't think the same. "It would have been nice to have them on ​court with ​us ⁠today, but here we are by ourselves. "We have worked incredibly hard and thank you all for appreciating that." pages.text: Tens of thousands of tents flooded after heavy rains in Gaza Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Weather Newsletters Tens of thousands of tents flooded after heavy rains in Gaza 7 November 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Emer Moreau Getty Images Ninety percent of Gaza residents have been displaced by the Israeli war against Hamas Heavy rains have flooded tens of thousands of tents where displaced residents have been living in Gaza, with a United Nations official saying almost everyone in the territory needs help. Residents used pots and pans to clear water from their flooded tents, with some saying they were left without shelter. Jonathan Veitch, the Unicef representative for Palestine, said the "desperate" situation was being made worse by Israeli restrictions on the entry of heavy machinery and supplies such as engine oil. Some 90% of Gaza residents have been displaced by the Israeli war against Hamas, many of them multiple times, with limited access to clean water and sanitation. Aid agencies say the situation is likely to worsen with the start of the rainy season. Speaking to the BBC from Deir Al Balah in central Gaza, Veitch said: "It's just horrific and they're absolutely desperate. "We're providing all the assistance that we can but we're getting stopped on the street as we're driving now because people are begging us for help." Testing and Diagnosis for Lyme disease For Everyone Nov. 2, 2026 Key points Healthcare providers consider multiple factors when evaluating a patient for Lyme disease. Laboratory diagnosis of Lyme disease relies on a blood test that detects antibodies to the Lyme bacteria. It can take several weeks after infection for the immune system to make enough antibodies to be detected by the test. CDC recommends using antibody tests that have been cleared by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and follow a two-step process. Some laboratories that do not accept private insurance may be offering tests that are not cleared by the FDA. Testing and Respiratory Viruses Aug. 18, 2025 Languages Español Español What to know Testing for respiratory viruses when you feel sick can help guide decisions to further protect yourself and others. Testing may be most helpful if you are at higher risk for getting very sick, so you can seek healthcare quickly and start treatment, if apporpriate. An additional strategy to further protect yourself and others View Larger Download Testing can provide useful information to help you make prevention or treatment choices. Testing for respiratory viruses can help you decide what to do next, like getting treatment to reduce your risk of severe illness and taking steps to lower your chances of spreading a virus to others. Experts blame falling vaccination rates. Madoff’s center first pointed to the concerning trend in a report published online late last year. pages.text: Thawing permafrost is threatening Svalbard's 'corpse point' | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE Thawing permafrost is threatening Svalbard's 'corpse point' Human bones and artifacts from the largest whalers’ graveyard in the archipelago are at risk of disintegrating. For centuries, the permafrost protected the graves of men who hunted whales in the Arctic. But coastal erosion and melting ice now threaten to decay their remains. Lise Loktu and Espen Olsen, Governor of Svalbard. By Kat Long Published July 28, 2026 More than 300 years ago, young men from all over Western Europe boarded ships bound for the Arctic. Under the unceasing light of polar summer, in a landscape of rock and ice, they hunted bowhead whales in the waters surrounding the Svalbard archipelago. The work was brutal; the wind unrelenting. Many never made it home. They were buried in whalers’ graveyards, fully dressed in their woolen jackets and knitted hats. Their shallow graves were marked with mounds of stones. In a paper published this past spring in PLOS One , she reported that climate change has helped damage the irreplaceable artifacts over the past four decades. pages.title: Thawing Permafrost May Have Created a New Type of Landslide, Which Could Become More Common as the World Warms
pages.description: Scientists call the events permafrost detachment slides. Instead of thawing from the top down, these landslides seem to originate from a weakened base
pages.text: Thawing Permafrost May Have Created a New Type of Landslide, Which Could Become More Common as the World Warms Skip to main content A scar left by the 2018 Redstone River permafrost landslide, one of the two events investigated in the new study. Adapted from J. M. Young et al., Geophysical Research Letters , 2026 In 2017 and 2018, a pair of strange landslides moved huge masses of rock and dirt in Canada’s Northwest Territories. The events occurred in the central Mackenzie Valley, and one of them even dammed a river and created a lake . The two natural disasters are part of a new class of landslides scientists are calling “permafrost detachment slides” in a study published in the journal Geophysical Research Letters in September. They may have been partially triggered by severe wildfires that occurred in 1995, which destabilized the ground and allowed the base of the permafrost to thaw. What’s more, these events may become more common as the planet continues to warm. “It’s a very dramatic manifestation of the changing climate,” says study co-author Joseph Young , a geoscientist who conducted the work at the University of Alberta in Canada, to Matt Simon at Grist . “They’ve only started happening in the last 10, 15 years, and it’s a very drastic and abrupt change in the landscape.” Young and his colleagues began the study after seeing something strange in the Northwest Territories in 2019. While conducting field research, they spotted large landslide scars in valleys that they knew were stable permafrost , or permanently frozen earth, reports Stephanie Pappas for Live Science

Wikimedia Commons One hundred and fifty-nine years ago, slave traders stole Lorna Gail Woods ’ great-great grandfather from what is now Benin in West Africa. Her ancestor, Charlie Lewis, was brutally ripped from his homeland, along with 109 other Africans, and brought to Alabama on the Clotilda , the last known slave ship to arrive in the United States. Today, researchers confirmed that the remains of that vessel, long rumored to exist but elusive for decades, have been found along the Mobile River, near 12 Mile Island and just north of the Mobile Bay delta. “The excitement and joy is overwhelming,” says Woods, in a voice trembling with emotion. The latest search for Amelia Earhart's plane centered on Nikumaroro, a remote atoll in the South Pacific. The island is at the center of a theory that Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan could have survived as castaways. Dubbed the “ Taraia Object ” after a nearby peninsula, it has tantalized researchers who believe Amelia Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan could have ended up on the remote atoll and survived as castaways. pages.text: The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning - BBC Sport By Jessica Abrahams BBC World Service Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in. She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet. Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes. The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space. It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles. Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race. Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons. So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend? Roman money, like this coin bearing the profile of Emperor Claudius, often contained silver, one of several precious metals that fueled Rome. The continent of North America has been inhabited by humans for at least 16,500 years. As early as the 1500s, early settlers and European thinkers were interested in discovering how humans had come to populate North and South America. One theory suggested the migration of Norsemen across Greenland into North America. Another theory proposed the island of Atlantis as the origins of human life in the New World. Yet another idea proposed that the inhabitants had generated out of mud. However, by the early 1800s, scientists and theorists began discussing the possibility of a land bridge that had spanned between Asia and North America thousands of years ago. For all of human history people have looked up to the inky blackness of night and marvelled at the stars. Anthony Brown, Alamy By Tristan Kennedy Published November 8, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Renowned for its distinctive skiing culture, Japan is the ultimate wish list destination for serious skiers and snowboarders. If you’re used to the slopes of Europe or North America, you’ll appreciate the small differences: in the menu at a mountain cafe, the particular etiquette of the onsen, or even the heated toilet seats; everything feels different in Japan. But the main claim to fame is its soft, lightweight and very consistent powder snow. Westerly winds whip off the Siberian tundra and scoop up moisture over the Sea of Japan, before dumping it as snow over the archipelago. This quirk of geography means that parts of the northern island of Hokkaido are blessed with up to 15 metres of snowfall every winter compared to, say, seven metres in European resorts such as Tignes, France. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn The Box Recreation Area | New Mexico View Map In Full Screen The 640-acre Box Recreation Area is a highly scenic, rugged area that is very popular for technical rock climbing and bouldering. The five cliffs on either side of this box canyon provide popular rock climbing for even highly skilled technical climbers. Challenging climbing opportunities include the Waterfall Wall, Corner Block, and the Fillet a Papillon Wall. Photos A woman climbs a rock face at The Box Recreation Area. Accessibility Description (ABA/ADA) There are limited facilities at The Box Recreation Area. Campsites are primitive, and visitors need to be able to walk for several yards across uneven dirt roads that lead uphill to access. The trail leading down into The Box is made of dirt, goes downhill, and dotted with rocks that may be a tripping hazard. The Box itself has several rock walls that offer climbing and bouldering for those of various skill levels. One needs to be able to set up safety gear, climb, hold one’s body weight with their hands and feet for extended periods of time, then repel down safely. pages.text: The Breakthrough Drugs Transforming Hemophilia Care | National Geographic Premium HEALTH The Breakthrough Drugs Transforming Hemophilia Care A new class of medicines offers steadier protection with fewer injections, while gene therapy is beginning to test the promise of a one-time treatment. Hemophilia is caused by missing clotting proteins that make it difficult for the body to stop bleeding. New medicines are now preventing most dangerous bleeds, while gene therapy may offer some patients years of protection after a single treatment. Steve Gschmeissner, Science Photo Library By Meryl Davids Landau Published October 7, 2026 When two of Sara Pavao’s sons were diagnosed with hemophilia soon after birth, she feared the blood-clotting disorder would limit their lives—or leave them disfigured. As young children, Kapono, now 18, and Duke, 13, bruised frequently. “They’d be black and blue down their shins, on their forearms, and even on their faces after bumping into things,” Pavao recalls. Today, the brothers surf six-foot waves near their home on Kauai, Hawaii, ride dirt bikes on the island’s trails, and practice jujitsu. Kapono also kickboxes and previously played baseball and skateboarded—activities that would have been unthinkable for many children with hemophilia just a few decades ago. Their freedom reflects a dramatic transformation in hemophilia care. The first major advance came with emicizumab , followed by several newer medicines introduced over the past two years. pages.text: The Case for Buying Kefir Over Yogurt | National Geographic Premium HEALTH The Case for Buying Kefir Over Yogurt The centuries-old drink is a microbiome powerhouse, packed with health benefits. In addition to its gut health benefits, kefir is also a good source of calcium, vitamin D, and protein. Rebecca Hale, NGM Staff By Meryl Davids Landau Published November 5, 2026 While kefir may have started as a potential accident centuries ago, scientists studying the increasingly popular fermented milk drink believe it may just live up to the hype (even if its origin stories likely do not). A review of more than two dozen human clinical trials published in March 2026 in the journal Healthcare concludes that consuming this probiotic-rich beverage offers small but meaningful improvements to the gut, the cardiovascular system, and even the mouth lining (which, like the intestines, is home to numerous good and bad bacteria). Kefir, the review states, is “a functional fermented milk beverage that can support human health on multiple levels.” Adding to the evidence are the test tube and animal studies documenting expanded microbe colonies in the gastrointestinal tract post consumption, along with other benefits such as improved cholesterol, immunity, and blood glucose regulation, a different review reported in February 2026 . ( Probiotics, Prebiotics, Postbiotics. What’s the Difference? ) “Kefir is a really wonderful drink from a health perspective,” says Jenna Smith, a registered dietitian and nutrition educator at the University of Illinois Extension. pages.text: The case for eating more organ meat | National Geographic Though often discarded, organ meats like kidney and liver offer much more nutrition than the muscle meat of an animal. Juan Moyano, Stocksy Premium HEALTH The case for eating more organ meat A growing body of research is proving that the often discarded portions of an animal are actually the most nutrient dense. By Mark Hay Published February 27, 2026 As a matter of pragmatism and genuine preference, cultures across the globe have long and storied histories of cooking with offal—a catch-all term for every part of an animal that isn’t a slab of muscle meat. Yet for all that history, over the last few decades, offal consumption has declined worldwide, says food scientist Carlos Álvarez, especially in developed countries like the United States. As the “mild” flavor (compared to other parts of the animal) and sanitized packaging of factory farmed muscle becomes the norm, explains Amy Bentley, a professor of food studies at New York University, eaters find the distinctive form, flavors, and textures of recognizable brains, tangy livers, and mushy glands increasing unnerving . But the disappearance of offal from modern foodways plays a part in food waste. Reports vary based on what their authors consider edible offal versus inedible items (some exclude bone, although much of it is edible), and which animal they examine. However, most livestock is between 12 to 44 percent offal by weight; a cow’s liver alone can account for up to 4.5 percent of its mass. ( The scientific case for eating more bones .) pages.text: The Colonies Come Together, Lesson 2 | Crash Course: American Revolution | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE CRASH COURSE The Colonies Come Together Lesson 2: Outraged by the Intolerable Acts, the Colonies decided to meet in Philadelphia on September 5, 1774, for the first Continental Congress. The crown’s harsh laws had backfired, reminding colonists that they were at the mercy of the whims of King George and his Parliament. Twelve of the Colonies sent delegates to Carpenters’ Hall, a brick building in central Philadelphia. Georgia declined to participate, wary of alienating the British as it faced threats from nearby Native American nations. East Florida and West Florida, then in the hands of the British, also did not participate. The First Continental Congress convened at Carpenters’ Hall in Philadelphia—a setting associated with common Americans—in September 1774 to debate how to respond to the Intolerable Acts that placed Massachusetts under military rule. Ann Broder, UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Fifty-six delegates arrived in total, including George Washington and John Adams from Virginia and Massachusetts, respectively. Though the delegates were galvanized by the injustice of the Intolerable Acts, many still considered themselves loyal subjects of the British crown. Joseph Galloway, a Pennsylvania delegate, even submitted a formal Plan of Union to create a colonial Parliament alongside the British Parliament.
